issues.issue: "Their affiliated chapter 11 debtors and debtors in possession" defines the released and bound "Debtors" only by reference to a footnote list that includes at least one non-U.S. entity (Aeropostale Canada Corp.), leaving the membership of the defined term arguable. The reach of every release and covenant turns on that boundary.
The defined term is opened but never closed ("the “Bankruptcy Court)"), a punctuation slip. It does not change the meaning, since the court is fully identified by name and case number.

The delivery obligation is measured by the Detailed Delivery Schedule attached as Exhibit A, but Section 7 requires the Debtors to file a "revised version of Exhibit A" on May 20, 2016, leaving it open which schedule fixes the delivery dates. Nothing states that the revised exhibit becomes the operative Detailed Delivery Schedule.

This fixes the Detailed Delivery Schedule as the May 9, 2016 summary sheet and excel support attached as Exhibit A, while Section 7 contemplates the Debtors filing a "revised version of Exhibit A" with the Settlement Motion. The two cannot both identify the controlling schedule without construction.

The five category terms ("Open Commitments," "Open CPOs", "Open Orders", "US Released for Delivery", "Orders in Transit") are given no content in the Agreement at all, being defined solely by whatever labels appear on an extrinsic spreadsheet. Because the 8% discount in Section 1(c) turns on which category a good falls in, the boundary between the categories is contestable.

MGF must accelerate deliveries or change shipping method "where possible", an undefined standard with no benchmark for what is possible or at what cost. Whether MGF has refused a permitted election or merely reached the limit of possibility would turn on that word.

The obligation to pay "full contract price" is immediately qualified by an 8.00% discount "applied on a pro rata basis to payments for the Goods from the first delivery to the last delivery", without specifying how the discount is spread across deliveries or whether it is measured by units or by dollars. Two different amortisation methods are equally available on the words.

"Front load ... to the extent practicable" and "minor ordinary course delays of less than two weeks consistent with past practice" are both open-textured, and the 10% discount trigger depends on the "original FOB turnover date" which is not fixed anywhere in the Agreement. Whether a discount is owed on any given licensee order is therefore genuinely arguable.

"No reductions and no cherry-picking" is colloquial and undefined, and the parenthetical then carves back in the Sourcing Agreement's adjustments for "defective product and similar adjustments" — a general catch-all against a specific example whose reach is uncertain. The line between a permitted quality adjustment and prohibited cherry-picking is left to be construed.

The cash-in-advance trigger depends on an "Event of Default (as defined in the DIP Financing)" and is then disapplied where the default was "caused by or related to" an MGF breach — "related to" is broad and undefined, and causation of a DIP default is rarely single-sourced. Which side bears the payment terms after a default would turn on that phrase.

The license is granted only on a "Full Chain Liquidation" of "all or substantially all" of the Debtors' stores or merchandise, and is lost if "the Court denies the proposed DIP Financing on a final basis based on the objection of" the Sycamore parties — both the "substantially all" threshold and what it means for a denial to be "based on" a particular objection are open. The license's existence turns on those undefined thresholds.

The license is styled "irrevocable" and is granted over goods to which title has not passed, yet Section 2 obliges the Debtors to take delivery of all Goods and Section 7 provides that the whole Agreement is "of no further force or effect" if no Settlement Order is entered by May 30, 2016. Whether an irrevocable license can survive that termination is a genuine question.

Carve-outs (b) and (c) preserve Claims against a Debtor Releasee "in any capacity other than as an employee, agent, officer and/or director of the Debtors", but the defined Debtor Releasees include the Debtors themselves, who have no such other capacity — so the carve-out's application to the Debtor entities is indeterminate. The reach of the general release against the corporate Debtors turns on that mismatch.

Carve-out (c) preserves only the ability to use MGF's conduct "in pursuing Claims against any MGF Releasees in any capacity other than as employees, agents, officers and directors of MGF", yet MGF itself has no other capacity and the persons the Debtors would in fact pursue (Sycamore and its affiliates) are not MGF Releasees at all. The scope of what conduct the Debtors may still use, and against whom, is left genuinely open.

This general release of MGF sits against Section 5(c), which says the general release does not extend to Sycamore Partners, Aero Investors, MGF Sourcing Holdings and their affiliates "even for conduct arising out of or relating to the released conduct of the MGF Releasees". Whether the Debtors may litigate MGF's released conduct as the predicate for claims against those non-released parties cannot be settled from 5(b) alone.

"Even for conduct arising out of or relating to the released conduct of the MGF Releasees" preserves claims against the Sycamore parties premised on conduct that has been released as against MGF, without saying how far the released actor's conduct may be proved or attributed. That is precisely the kind of phrase two sides read differently.

This preservation is hard to square with the carve-out in Section 5(b)(c), which permits the Debtors to use MGF's conduct only "in pursuing Claims against any MGF Releasees" — a narrower permission than 5(c) appears to assume. Harmonising the two requires construction.

The release is said not to affect "the amount of the obligations" under the Term Loan, which by expressio unius leaves open whether it affects the priority, validity or subordination of those obligations. Preserving amount alone is a conspicuously narrow specific in a clause otherwise cast as an avoidance-of-doubt saving.

Section 5(c) states the general release does not extend to Aero Investors LLC (the Term Loan administrative agent) or its affiliates at all, while 5(d) protects only the "amount" of the Term Loan obligations; the two savings provisions do not draw the same line. Their interaction on claims touching the Term Loan needs construing.

The parties waive California Civil Code section 1542 in an agreement that Section 8(l) makes governed by New York law without regard to conflicts principles, so the waiver's operative effect on the scope of the releases in 5(a) and 5(b) is uncertain. It is nevertheless a common belt-and-braces recital and unlikely to be outcome-determinative.

The termination fee, shortfall and rebate provisions cease "as of the date that the Settlement Order ... becomes a final order", but "final order" is nowhere defined and could mean entry, expiry of the appeal period, or exhaustion of appeals. The timing of the waiver of those claims turns on that term.

Automatic termination of the Sourcing Agreement on last delivery and final payment must be read with Section 8(m), which keeps the Sourcing Agreement "in full force and effect until terminated in accordance with this Agreement", and with Section 7's provision that the whole Agreement may become of no force. Which document governs residual obligations after that point is not spelled out.

The survival proviso preserves "MGF's obligation to provide 14 day payment terms", but Section 3 casts the fourteen-day term as the Debtors' payment obligation, not an MGF obligation, and the Settlement Order must be "in form and substance reasonably acceptable to MGF" — an undefined standard giving MGF a contestable veto. Whether the Agreement fell away turns on those words.

The requirement to file a "revised version of Exhibit A" cannot be squared with Section 1(a), which fixes the Detailed Delivery Schedule as the May 9, 2016 materials attached as Exhibit A. Which version measures MGF's delivery obligations is left unresolved.

The confidentiality duty attaches to "pricing information contained in the Detailed Delivery Schedule" and requires "all reasonable actions necessary" to seal it "to the extent possible" — both the boundary of what counts as pricing information and the level of effort are undefined. Litigation over a disclosure would turn on those phrases.

The clause is built on layered undefined standards — "reasonably cooperate", "ordinary course business channels", "minor delays", "materially impact", "reasonable business efforts, whenever possible" — none measured against any benchmark. Whether a party has failed to cooperate is scarcely capable of decision without construing them.

The consent requirement extends to "any commentary with respect to any of MGF and/or its affiliates and/or the Debtors" "with respect to this Agreement or its terms and conditions", a sweep broad enough to capture ordinary court filings and disclosures that the Agreement elsewhere contemplates. Its outer edge is genuinely uncertain.

The clause says a waiver of one breach is not a waiver of "any other provision or condition", but is silent on whether waiving one breach waives a later breach of the same provision — the ordinary formulation. That omission leaves a gap a party could exploit.

The integration clause makes the Agreement, the Detailed Delivery Schedule and the Sourcing Agreement as modified the entire agreement, yet Sections 6 and 8(m) leave the Sourcing Agreement's own terms operating and Section 2 imports its adjustment provisions. Which document controls where the two texts differ is not stated.

The proviso requires consent of "both any required lenders and the Agent" for any amendment "adverse to the interests of the lenders party to the DIP Financing" — whether an amendment is adverse to lender interests is a judgment call with no stated test. An amendment's validity would turn on it.

This says nothing in the Agreement alters the DIP Financing, while Section 3 changes the Debtors' payment terms by reference to Events of Default under the DIP Financing and Section 8(g) conditions amendments on lender consent. Whether the payment mechanics amount to a prohibited alteration is arguable, though the clauses can probably be read together.

The releases are made binding on an enumerated list — purchasers, liquidation agents, reorganized Debtors, chapter 11 or 7 trustees — closed by the catch-all "any other successor to the Debtors", whose reach against the specifics is uncertain under ejusdem generis. Whether a particular third party is bound turns on that catch-all.

"All things reasonably necessary, or as may be reasonably requested" to carry out the "purposes and intent" of the Agreement is an open-ended obligation with no benchmark, capable of being urged as a freestanding duty. Its boundary against the specific obligations elsewhere is undefined.

New York law is chosen without regard to conflicts principles, yet Section 5(e) has the parties waive a California statute (Civil Code section 1542). The interaction is odd but almost certainly harmonised as a belt-and-braces release term.

The Sourcing Agreement is said to remain in full force "until terminated in accordance with this Agreement", but Section 6 already strips out its termination fee, shortfall and rebate provisions and Section 7 lets the whole Agreement lapse if no Settlement Order is entered — leaving the status of the Sourcing Agreement in that event unaddressed. Reconciling the survival of the Sourcing Agreement across those scenarios requires construction.
